overview: Visualization is not about making charts look good — it is about thinking. Visualization is a cognitive tool, not an output artifact. It reveals what statistics cannot surface immediately, what models may hide, and what metrics may average away.
This module covers why visualization matters, Matplotlib basics, Seaborn statistical plots, and visualizing model results — essential skills for data exploration and model diagnosis.

topics.title: Why Visualization Matters
theory: Humans are excellent at pattern recognition but poor at interpreting raw numbers. Visualization leverages spatial reasoning, color perception, and shape recognition to see trends, detect outliers, spot relationships, and identify errors.

Visualization appears at every stage: data acquisition (are values realistic?), EDA (what patterns exist?), feature engineering (which features matter?), model evaluation (where does the model fail?), and communication (can insights be trusted?).

Statistics quantifies and aggregates; visualization reveals structure and exposes anomalies. Example: Mean accuracy = 92% hides that one class is failing completely. Without visualization, models can lie convincingly.

Visualization prevents silent failures: data leakage, label imbalance, skewed distributions, train-test contamination. It exposes these early. The cost of skipping visualization is misleading metrics and fragile systems.
visualIntuition: Anscombe's Quartet: four datasets with identical statistics but completely different patterns when visualized.
visualSuggestions: Same metric, different underlying distributions comparison

code.content:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

# Always visualize before modeling
data = np.random.randn(1000)

plt.hist(data, bins=30)
plt.title("Distribution Check")
plt.show()

topics.title: Matplotlib Basics
theory: Matplotlib is fundamental because it is primitive — it gives full control over every visual element. Higher-level libraries (Seaborn, Plotly) sit on top of it and abstract decisions away.
Matplotlib follows a hierarchical model: Figure (canvas) → Axes (coordinate system) → Plot elements. Most confusion comes from mixing Figure and Axes concepts.

Pyplot interface (plt.plot()) is state-based — good for exploration but limited for complex layouts. Object-oriented interface (fig, ax = plt.subplots()) provides explicit control and is preferred for production.

Basic plot types serve different purposes: Line plots for trends/time series, scatter plots for relationships, bar plots for categorical comparison, histograms for distributions. Choose plot based on what question you're answering.
visualIntuition: Figure hierarchy diagram: Figure contains Axes, which contains plot elements, labels, ticks, and legends.
visualSuggestions: Same data shown with different plot types

code.content:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

x = np.linspace(0, 10, 100)
y = np.sin(x)

# Object-oriented interface (preferred)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(x, y)
ax.set_xlabel("X")
ax.set_ylabel("sin(X)")
ax.set_title("Sine Wave")
plt.show()

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(10, 8))

# Line plot
axs[0, 0].plot([1, 2, 3, 4], [1, 4, 2, 3])
axs[0, 0].set_title("Line Plot")

# Scatter plot
axs[0, 1].scatter(np.random.randn(50), np.random.randn(50))
axs[0, 1].set_title("Scatter Plot")

# Bar plot
axs[1, 0].bar(['A', 'B', 'C'], [3, 7, 5])
axs[1, 0].set_title("Bar Plot")

# Histogram
axs[1, 1].hist(np.random.randn(1000), bins=30)
axs[1, 1].set_title("Histogram")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

topics.title: Seaborn Statistical Plots
theory: Matplotlib shows how to draw; Seaborn shows what to draw. Seaborn is built for statistical thinking and dataset-aware visualization. It encodes statistical defaults so users focus on meaning, not mechanics.
Seaborn expects a DataFrame with column names and semantic roles (x, y, hue). Visualization becomes declarative: what varies, what is compared, what is grouped.

Distribution plots (histplot, boxplot, violinplot) reveal spread, skewness, multimodality. Relationship plots (regplot, pairplot) show dependency and correlation. Categorical plots (countplot, barplot) compare groups.

Heatmaps compress large matrices into pattern perception — used for correlation analysis, confusion matrices, feature interactions. Faceting (FacetGrid) enables comparison across subsets without overplotting.
visualIntuition: Seaborn's data-centric model: DataFrame columns map directly to visual properties (x, y, hue, size).

code.content:
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Load example dataset
df = sns.load_dataset('tips')

# Distribution with KDE
sns.histplot(df['total_bill'], kde=True)
plt.title("Bill Distribution")
plt.show()

# Relationship with regression line
sns.regplot(x='total_bill', y='tip', data=df)
plt.show()

# Categorical comparison
sns.boxplot(x='day', y='total_bill', data=df)
plt.show()

import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = sns.load_dataset('iris')

# Correlation heatmap
corr = df.corr()
sns.heatmap(corr, annot=True, cmap='coolwarm')
plt.title("Feature Correlations")
plt.show()

# Pairplot for EDA
sns.pairplot(df, hue='species')
plt.show()

topics.title: Visualizing Model Results
theory: Metrics compress behavior into numbers; visualization reveals behavior. A model with high accuracy can still fail on edge cases, be biased, overfit specific regions, and generalize poorly.

Regression diagnostics: Predicted vs Actual plot (perfect predictions on diagonal), Residual plot (reveals non-linearity, heteroscedasticity, missing features), Residual distribution (checks for bias and extreme errors).

Classification diagnostics: Confusion matrix (shows what the model confuses), Probability distribution (reveals overconfidence), ROC curve (threshold-independent performance), Precision-Recall curve (important for imbalanced classes).

Learning curves show bias-variance tradeoff and whether more data helps. Feature importance shows what the model relies on. Never tune hyperparameters before understanding failure modes through visualization.
visualIntuition: Model diagnosis framework: predictions vs reality, error patterns, confidence calibration, failure mode analysis.
visualSuggestions: Residual plot showing structured vs random residuals

code.content:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

y_true = np.array([3, -0.5, 2, 7])
y_pred = np.array([2.5, 0.0, 2, 8])
residuals = y_true - y_pred

fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))

# Predicted vs Actual
axs[0].scatter(y_true, y_pred)
axs[0].plot([min(y_true), max(y_true)], [min(y_true), max(y_true)], 'r--')
axs[0].set_xlabel("Actual")
axs[0].set_ylabel("Predicted")
axs[0].set_title("Predicted vs Actual")

# Residual plot
axs[1].scatter(y_pred, residuals)
axs[1].axhline(0, color='r', linestyle='--')
axs[1].set_xlabel("Predicted")
axs[1].set_ylabel("Residual")
axs[1].set_title("Residual Plot")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix
import numpy as np

y_true = np.array([0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0])
y_pred = np.array([0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0])

cm = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred)
sns.heatmap(cm, annot=True, fmt='d', cmap='Blues')
plt.xlabel("Predicted")
plt.ylabel("Actual")
plt.title("Confusion Matrix")
plt.show()

topics.title: Plotly Express — Interactive Charts
topics.theory:
Plotly Express is a high-level API for creating interactive charts with minimal code. It supports scatter, bar, line, histogram, box, heatmap, and 3D plots with built-in tooltips, zooming, and panning.

**Key features:** Color-coding by category, bubble charts (size parameter), log scales, hover data, and automatic legends. Templates like `plotly_white` and `plotly_dark` provide instant styling.

**Chart types:** `px.scatter` (relationship), `px.bar` (comparison), `px.line` (trends), `px.histogram` (distribution), `px.box` (spread), `px.imshow` (heatmaps), `px.scatter_3d` (3D exploration).

code.title: Plotly Express — Scatter, Bar, Histogram, Heatmap
code.code:
import plotly.express as px
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

np.random.seed(42)
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'x': np.random.randn(200),
    'y': np.random.randn(200),
    'category': np.random.choice(['A','B','C'], 200),
    'size': np.random.uniform(5, 50, 200)
})

# Scatter with color and size
fig = px.scatter(df, x='x', y='y', color='category',
    size='size', hover_data=['category'],
    title='Interactive Scatter Plot')
fig.show()

# Histogram with marginal rug
fig = px.histogram(df, x='x', color='category',
    marginal='rug', barmode='overlay', opacity=0.7)
fig.show()

# Correlation heatmap
corr = df[['x','y','size']].corr()
fig = px.imshow(corr, color_continuous_scale='RdBu_r',
    zmin=-1, zmax=1, text_auto='.2f')
fig.show()

visualSuggestions: Live Plotly chart embedded with interactive controls
Chart type selector showing the same data in different plot types
visualIntuition: Plotly Express is like Instagram filters for data — one line of code transforms raw numbers into an interactive, zoomable, tooltipped chart.

topics.title: Subplots and Layout Customisation
topics.theory:
Plotly's `make_subplots` creates multi-panel figures with shared axes, mixed chart types, and precise layout control.

**Key parameters:** `rows`/`cols` for grid, `shared_xaxes`/`shared_yaxes` for linked axes, `specs` for mixed types.

**Layout features:** `hovermode='x unified'` links tooltips across subplots, `dragmode` controls interaction (zoom/pan/select/lasso), `template` sets visual theme.

**Annotations & shapes:** `add_vline`, `add_hline`, `add_annotation` for marking important points, thresholds, or events.

code.title: Multi-panel Subplots with Shared Axes
code.code:
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import numpy as np

x = np.arange(12)
y1 = np.random.randint(100, 500, 12)
y2 = np.random.randint(20, 100, 12)

fig = make_subplots(rows=2, cols=1,
    subplot_titles=['Revenue', 'Units Sold'],
    shared_xaxes=True, vertical_spacing=0.12)

fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=x, y=y1, name='Revenue'), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=x, y=y2, name='Units', fill='tozeroy'), row=2, col=1)

fig.update_layout(title='Sales Dashboard',
    hovermode='x unified', template='plotly_white', height=500)
fig.add_hline(y=300, line_dash='dash', line_color='red',
    annotation_text='Target', row=1, col=1)
fig.show()

visualSuggestions: Dashboard mockup with multiple linked panels
visualIntuition: Subplots are like a newspaper layout — each panel tells a different aspect of the same story. Shared axes link them together.

topics.title: Interactive Controls and Export
topics.theory:
Plotly supports buttons, dropdowns, range sliders, and range selectors for building dashboard-like interactivity without a web framework.

**Range slider:** Essential for time series — `rangeslider_visible=True` adds a zoomable overview bar.

**Update buttons:** `method='update'` changes trace visibility; `method='relayout'` changes axis properties (e.g., linear vs log scale).

**Export:** `.write_html()` for interactive HTML, `.write_image()` for static PNG/PDF/SVG (requires kaleido).

code.title: Range Selectors, Dropdowns, and Export
code.code:
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

dates = pd.date_range('2023-01-01', periods=365, freq='D')
values = np.cumsum(np.random.randn(365)) + 100

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=dates, y=values, name='Price'))

fig.update_xaxes(
    rangeslider_visible=True,
    rangeselector=dict(buttons=[
        dict(count=7, label='1W', step='day', stepmode='backward'),
        dict(count=1, label='1M', step='month', stepmode='backward'),
        dict(count=3, label='3M', step='month', stepmode='backward'),
        dict(step='all', label='All')
    ]))

fig.update_layout(
    updatemenus=[dict(buttons=[
        dict(label='Linear', method='relayout', args=[{'yaxis.type': 'linear'}]),
        dict(label='Log', method='relayout', args=[{'yaxis.type': 'log'}])
    ])],
    title='Interactive Time Series', template='plotly_white')
fig.show()

visualSuggestions: Time series with working range slider and scale toggle
visualIntuition: Interactive controls turn a static chart into a data exploration tool. The range slider is like a telescope — you control the zoom level and focal point.

quiz.question: Why does visualization matter before modeling?
options: It reveals data patterns, outliers, and distributions that summary statistics miss
quiz.explanation: Anscombe's Quartet shows 4 datasets with identical summary statistics but vastly different patterns. Only visualization reveals the true structure. Always plot before computing.

quiz.question: When should you use Seaborn over Matplotlib?
options: When you need statistical plots with less code — Seaborn provides higher-level abstractions for common patterns
quiz.explanation: Seaborn wraps Matplotlib with sensible defaults and specialized statistical plots (violin, pair, heatmap). Use Matplotlib for full control and custom layouts; Seaborn for quick, publication-quality statistical visualizations.

quiz.question: What does a correlation heatmap reveal?
options: Pairwise linear relationships between features — useful for identifying redundancy and multicollinearity
quiz.explanation: Correlation heatmaps show Pearson or Spearman coefficients between all feature pairs. High correlation indicates redundancy (potentially drop one). But correlation ≠ causation, and it only captures linear relationships.

quiz.question: Why should you visualize model results, not just accuracy numbers?
options: Residual plots and confusion matrices reveal systematic errors that aggregate metrics hide
quiz.explanation: A model with 90% accuracy might systematically fail on a specific subgroup. Residual plots reveal non-random error patterns. Confusion matrices show exactly which classes are confused. Numbers alone hide these patterns.

quiz.question: Which Plotly Express function creates an interactive correlation heatmap?
quiz.explanation: px.imshow() displays matrix data as a heatmap. With text_auto=True it creates an annotated correlation heatmap.

quiz.question: What does `hovermode='x unified'` do in Plotly?
options: Shows only x-axis values on hover
Links tooltips across all traces at the same x position
Unifies all hover text into one line
quiz.explanation: The 'x unified' hovermode shows a single consolidated tooltip for all traces at the same x-coordinate, making it easy to compare values.
